summary: This unit teaches you to keep each guest's account correct from check-in to check-out: open the folio, post charges from signed slips, take payments and deposits in J$ and US$, make paid-outs, correct errors with the right approval, watch credit limits, and protect the privacy and security of the account. You will also learn how company accounts, split folios and the night audit work.

blocks.p: Every guest who stays at a villa, guest house or hotel spends money there: on the room, meals, drinks, laundry, tours and more. The front office keeps a running record of what each guest owes and what they have paid. That record is the **guest account**, and it is the front office's most important financial job. If it is wrong, the villa loses money, or the guest is overcharged and leaves unhappy.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees who work at the front desk or in the office. You will work with a paper folio or a front office computer system, and with numbers. Accuracy, honesty and privacy matter more here than speed.

flow: Open the folio at check-in

Post payments and deposits
Check and correct

Final check, settle and close at check-out

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's front office. In the practical tasks you post a day's charges to made-up folios and balance them, then do a credit check, a split folio and role plays with guests and callers. The assessor watches your accuracy, your checking and your care with private information.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: All practical work uses made-up folios, made-up names and made-up exchange rates. Never use a real guest's details or a real card number in practice work or in photographs.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: What a guest account is and how it is opened

blocks.p: A **folio** is the record of one guest's (or one payer's) **charges** and **payments** during a stay. A charge is something the guest buys and owes. A payment is money the guest gives, and it reduces what is owed. The result is the **balance**.

head: Word
What it means
Example
rows: Charge (debit)
An amount the guest owes: it makes the balance higher.
Room charge for the night; dinner; laundry.
Payment (credit)
An amount the guest has paid: it makes the balance lower.
A deposit; cash at the desk; a card payment.
Balance
Charges minus payments: what the guest still owes.
Charges J$38,000, payments J$25,000: balance J$13,000.
Credit balance
The guest has paid more than the charges, so the property owes the guest.
Charges US$420, deposit US$500: US$80 credit to the guest.

blocks.h: A folio on paper or on screen

ul: A folio shows the guest's name, room number, arrival and departure dates, rate, folio number, and the payer.
Each line shows the **date**, the **department** (rooms, restaurant, bar, laundry, tours), a short description, the **amount**, and the slip number.
At the bottom it shows total charges, total payments and the balance.

Many properties use a **property management system (PMS)**: one computer system for reservations, rooms and accounts. Restaurants and bars may use a **point of sale (POS)** terminal that sends charges straight to the room folio. Small villas may still use paper folios and a cash book. The rules are the same.

head: Ledger
Holds the accounts of
Notes
rows: Guest ledger (front office ledger)
Guests staying in the property now.
Open accounts that change every day.
City ledger (non-guest ledger)
Companies, agents and others who are billed later, and guests who have left with an amount still owing.
The bill is sent by invoice. Also called accounts receivable.

flow: Greet the guest and find the booking
Check the guest's identity (passport or other photo ID)
Confirm the rate, dates and who pays what
Ask for a way to pay: a deposit already paid, or a card for a pre-authorisation
Set the credit limit as the property's policy says
Guest signs the registration card
Open the folio and link any deposit or company arrangement
Give the guest the room key and explain how charges will be billed

head: Term
What it means
Why it matters
rows: Deposit (advance payment)
Money the guest paid before arrival, often to confirm the booking.
Posted as a **payment (credit)**. It lowers the balance. It is not a charge.
Pre-authorisation
A hold placed on the guest's card for an amount that covers expected charges.
It is **not a payment**. The money is only held. The real charge is made at check-out for the amount owed, and the hold is released.
Credit limit
The most a guest may owe before the front office asks for a payment.
Set by the property's policy, often by the length of stay, the room rate and the way of paying.
Walk-in
A guest who arrives without a booking.
Check photo ID and a way to pay before you open an account for charging meals to the room.

blocks.note: Never open a charge account for a guest you cannot identify, and never take a guest's word that someone else will pay. Get it in writing or check the company's agreement first.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Posting** means adding a charge to the right guest's account. Charges come from the restaurant, bar, minibar, laundry, spa, tours and other departments, usually as a **charge slip** (also called a voucher or chit). The guest signs the slip to agree the charge goes on the room account.

blocks.h: Check the slip before you post

head: Check
Why
rows: Guest name and room number match
A wrong room number puts a charge on the wrong guest, the most common posting error.
The date is today's (or the correct day)
Charges must fall on the right day for the audit and for the guest's bill.
The amount is clear and the sum is right
Unclear figures and wrong additions cause disputes.
The guest's signature is there
It proves the guest agreed. No signature: ask the department to get it, or follow the property's rule.
The department and a description are shown
So the charge goes to the right department line.
The charge is not already posted
Posting a slip twice overcharges the guest.

flow: Take the slip and check it (name, room, date, amount, signature)
Find the guest's folio and confirm it is open and the name matches
Choose the right department code
Key in the amount exactly as written, with the slip number
Compare the posting on the screen with the slip, line by line
Mark the slip as posted (initials and date) and file it with the day's records

ul: **Post as soon as you can.** A late posting may be missed at check-out and become a **late charge**.
**Keep the signed slip.** It is the proof if a guest asks about the charge. Keep it with the day's records, as the property says. Do not throw it away because it is on the system.
**Check by comparing the posting with the signed slip**, not by asking the guest whether it looks about right and not by waiting for the night audit to find errors.

blocks.h: Room charges, taxes and service charge

ul: The **room charge** is usually posted automatically to every occupied room by the **night audit**, at the rate agreed at check-in.

**GCT (General Consumption Tax)** is a tax on goods and services. Use the **current rate set by law**; the property's system or your supervisor tells you the rate. Never use a rate you remember from last year or one a guest suggests.

Some properties add a **service charge** (a percentage the property sets). Prices shown to guests should make clear whether tax and service charge are included. Tell the guest before the service, at booking or at check-in, never only at the end.
Work out room charges carefully. Example: J$18,000 a night for 3 nights is 3 × J$18,000 = J$54,000 before tax.

blocks.p: Mr Devon Powell is in Room 4. His folio shows a room charge of J$20,000 for tonight (posted by the night audit). During the day these signed slips arrive: restaurant J$5,600, bar J$2,400, laundry J$1,900. He paid a J$25,000 deposit at booking.

head: Line
Charge (J$)
Payment (J$)
rows: Room charge
Restaurant
Bar
Laundry
Deposit
Totals

blocks.p: Balance = 29,900 − 25,000 = **J$4,900 owing**. Always add the charges, add the payments, then take one from the other, and check your answer a second way.

blocks.h: Control: do the day's slips match the day's postings?

blocks.p: At the end of a shift, add up the slips you received and compare them with the total posted on the **daily posting control sheet** or the system report. If the totals differ, find out why before you hand over: a slip may be missing, posted twice, posted for the wrong amount or posted to the wrong guest.

blocks.note: Typing errors are common. A **transposition** is two digits swapped (J$2,350 keyed as J$3,250). A difference that divides exactly by 9 is a clue that digits may have been swapped. Always compare with the slip.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Payments, deposits, paid-outs and foreign money

head: Method
What you do
What you check
rows: Cash (J$ or US$)
Count it with the guest, post it, give a receipt, put it in the drawer.
The notes look genuine, as the property's check says
The amount counted aloud matches what you post
Give correct change
Credit or debit card
Use the card terminal; post the payment when approved.
The amount keyed is exactly the amount owed
The guest signs or enters a PIN
Give the guest the card and the slip
Deposit already paid
Post as a payment when received; take it into account at check-out.
The right booking and amount
A receipt was given
Company or agent
Charge the agreed items to the company account (city ledger).
Written approval from the company
Exactly which charges it pays
Bank transfer or other methods
Only as the property's policy allows.
Money has really arrived before the account is cleared

ul: Never put cash in your pocket 'until later'. Count it with the guest and post it at once. Give a receipt every time, not only when the guest asks.
If a **card is declined**, tell the guest quietly and privately and ask for another way to pay. Do not keep trying the card again and again, and never announce it in the lobby.
Never write down a guest's full card number or the security code. Where card details must be kept, follow the property's secure method.

blocks.p: A **paid-out** is money the property pays out for a guest and adds to the guest's account. Example: the guest asks you to pay a taxi driver J$3,000 or a delivery boy for a package. A paid-out is often written as **VPO** (visitor paid out).

flow: Check that the guest agrees: ask them to sign a paid-out slip
Take the money from the cash drawer only as the property's rules allow
Get a receipt from the person you pay
Post the amount to the guest's folio as a charge, with the slip and receipt attached
Record it in the cash book or the front office log

blocks.note: A paid-out needs two papers: the guest's signature and the receipt from the person paid. Without them, the property cannot prove the money was spent for the guest.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Many guests carry US dollars. Accounts at most properties are kept in J$, although some villas show rates in US$. When a guest pays in US$ towards a J$ account, you convert at **the property's rate for that day**. The rate is set by the property (it changes every day, and it is posted at the desk or in the system). It is not a newspaper rate, not a rate the guest says is fair and not a rate chosen because it is easy to calculate.

head: To change
Calculation
Example (made-up rate US$1 = J$155)
rows: US$ to J$
US$ amount × rate
J$ to US$
J$ amount ÷ rate

ul: Check where the decimal point goes. US$100 at J$155 is **J$15,500**, not J$1,550 or J$155,000.
If a guest pays only part in US$, post the J$ value of the US$ received, then work out the remaining J$ balance.
On the receipt, show the US$ received, the rate used and the J$ value credited. Keep the rate on the folio.

blocks.p: Worked example, with a made-up rate of US$1 = J$158: the bill is J$63,200 and the guest pays US$300 cash. US$300 × 158 = J$47,400 credited. The balance is 63,200 − 47,400 = **J$15,800**, which the guest pays by card. Check: 47,400 + 15,800 = 63,200.

blocks.note: The rates in this kit are made up for practice. In real work, always use the property's rate for the day from the desk or the system.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Corrections, allowances, transfers and company accounts

blocks.h: Mistakes happen: how you deal with them

blocks.p: Everybody posts a wrong amount or the wrong room sometimes. What matters is how you deal with it. You must **never delete an entry and say nothing**, and never leave a mistake in the hope the guest will not notice. Every correction must leave a clear trail.

head: Type of error
How you correct it
rows: Charge posted to the wrong room or guest
Transfer or move it to the right folio with a recorded reason (a correcting entry), and tell your supervisor as the property says. If the wrong guest was told the amount, apologise.
Wrong amount keyed (including a transposition)
Post an **adjustment** for the difference, with a note of why, and keep the slip.
Charge posted twice
Post an adjustment for the duplicate, with the reason.
Guest did not take the item or service (disputed or overcharged)
Check the evidence first. If the charge is to come off, it needs a supervisor's or manager's approval. Post an **allowance** with the reason.

head: Word
What it means
rows: Adjustment
A change that corrects a wrong amount or entry.
Allowance (rebate)
An amount taken off a guest's account to correct an overcharge or to make up for poor service. It needs approval from a supervisor or manager.
Transfer
Moving a charge from one folio to another (for example to the right room or to a company account).
Audit trail
The record of every posting and correction, showing when it was made and who made it.

ul: Record every correction with the **date, the reason and your name or login**. This lets anyone check it later.
Only a **supervisor or manager** approves allowances, discounts and write-offs, never any staff member who happens to be free and never the housekeeper or the guest next door.
If a guest says a staff member promised a discount (such as 20%), do not simply give it and do not refuse rudely: check with your supervisor first.
If a guest **moves from one room to another**, the same account moves with them. The folio goes to the new room with all its charges. Do not open a new account and delete the old one.
If **two guests in different rooms agree that one will pay for both**, get both to agree in writing, then transfer the charges. Never move charges without both guests' agreement.

blocks.h: Company accounts, master folios and split folios

blocks.p: Sometimes someone other than the guest pays for part of the stay: a company for its staff member, a tour operator for a group, an agent. This is arranged **before** the guest arrives, in writing.

head: Term
What it means
Example
rows: Master folio (master account)
One main account that collects all the charges a company or group has agreed to pay.
A tour company pays for the group's rooms: one master folio for all the rooms.
Split folio
Two or more folios for one guest, each with a different payer.
Folio A (the company): room and tax. Folio B (the guest): meals, drinks and laundry.
City ledger transfer
Moving the part the company will pay to the city ledger at check-out, for an invoice later.
The company's folio goes to the city ledger; the guest settles folio B at the desk.

flow: Check the company's written approval and exactly what it covers
At check-in, set up two folios (company and guest) and mark which charges go where
Post each charge to the right folio as it arrives
At check-out, the guest checks and pays the personal folio
Send the company folio to the city ledger with the approval letter and the signed slips

blocks.note: Before a bill goes to a company, the front office must hold the company's written approval. Never charge a company on the guest's word alone.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Credit control, the night audit and late charges

blocks.p: Credit control means making sure that the amount a guest owes does not grow bigger than the guest can pay. The property sets a **credit limit** for each account when it opens. A pre-authorisation or deposit helps to cover it.

ul: Check balances every day, or run a **high balance report**. This report lists guests whose balance is **near or over** their limit.

When a guest is near or over the limit, **tell your supervisor** and follow the property's policy. A common action is for the supervisor or the desk to speak to the guest privately and ask for a payment or a higher card hold.
Do not lock a guest out of the room, do not ignore the problem until the day the guest leaves, and do not discuss it with other guests or in public.

head: Situation
Usual action
rows: Balance is near the limit
Tell the supervisor; the guest may be asked for a payment or a higher card hold.
Balance is over the limit
Tell the supervisor at once; speak to the guest privately and politely.
A card hold has been used up
Ask for another payment as policy says.
Guest is not seen at the desk and the balance is high
Report it so that the supervisor can decide what to do.

blocks.p: The **night audit** is done at the end of the business day, often by a night auditor. Its main purpose is to **check all postings and balance the day's accounts**.

flow: Check that every department's slips and reports have arrived
Compare the departments' totals with what was posted to folios
Find and correct any differences
Post the room charge for the night to every occupied room
Print or save the day's reports (including the high balance report)
Roll the system on to the next date

ul: The audit trail shows who made each posting, so errors can be traced.
**On the evening before a guest leaves**, check the guest's folio so that any errors are found and fixed before check-out, not when the guest is waiting at the desk with a flight to catch.

blocks.p: A **late charge** is a charge that reaches the front desk **after the guest has checked out**, for example a bar slip that arrives an hour after the guest left.

ul: **Prevent them.** Ask the guest at check-out if they have had breakfast, a minibar drink or anything else this morning. Ask departments to send slips quickly. Check the minibar before the guest leaves, as policy says.

**If one arrives**, do not throw it away, do not pay it yourself and do not post it to the next guest in the room. Report it and follow the property's **late charge policy**. The policy may allow a charge to a card the guest agreed could be used, or may say the amount is written off. Your supervisor decides.

blocks.p: A guest who leaves without paying is called a **skipper**. If you think a guest may have left without settling the bill, **report it to your supervisor at once**. Do not chase the guest yourself.

head: Warning sign
What you do
rows: The balance is high and the guest is not at the desk
Report it to the supervisor.
The guest's luggage has gone and the folio is unpaid
Report it at once.
The card hold has failed or was released
Tell your supervisor and follow the policy.

blocks.p: A guest's account holds private details: the guest's name, room, spending, card information and sometimes whom they are with. Guests trust the villa with these details. Giving them to the wrong person can put a guest in danger, harm the guest's privacy and damage the villa's name.

head: Situation
What you do
rows: A guest at the desk asks for a printout or to see their folio
Check that they are the registered guest (ask for their name and key card, or ID), then print or show it.
A caller says she is the guest and asks for her balance
Do not give details until you have checked she is the guest, as the property's policy says. For example, ask her to come to the desk, or ask questions only the guest could answer.
A visitor asks what another guest has spent
Say politely that you cannot share a guest's account details.
A person says they are a guest's friend, wife or colleague and asks for the bill
Do not give it. Offer to take a message or ask the guest to contact them.
A guest staying for two weeks asks for the charges so far
Print or show the folio after checking it is the guest. Do not make them wait until check-out.

ul: **Log off or lock the screen** when you leave the desk, even for a few minutes. Never turn the screen so guests in the lobby can read it.

**Never share your password.** Every posting is linked to the person who logged in. If a colleague uses your login, you are responsible for what they do. Never write your password on a note by the keyboard.
Keep folios, slips and registration cards in a locked drawer or office, not on the desk where passers-by can read them.
Never write down full card numbers or security codes. Hand terminals only to guests who must enter their PIN. A **PIN** is a personal identification number.
Shred or securely destroy papers with card or personal details when the rules allow it.

blocks.note: Never say aloud a guest's room number, balance or card details where others can hear. If you must discuss money, do it quietly at the desk or in the office.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A guest may disagree with a charge: 'I did not have lunch here' or 'Nobody told me about that charge'. Stay calm. The guest may be right, and even when the guest is wrong, how you handle it decides whether they come back.

flow: Listen without interrupting and thank the guest for raising it
Check the **signed slip** with the guest, quietly and privately
If the slip shows the guest's signature, explain the charge calmly
If it is clear the charge is wrong, apologise and correct it with the right approval
If you cannot settle it, ask your supervisor to join you
Record the query and what was done

ul: Do not say 'the system is never wrong', and do not remove the charge at once without checking.
Do not argue and do not ask the guest to pay now and complain later.
A **minibar** charge the guest disputes: check the housekeeper's minibar sheet and the slip; any allowance still needs the supervisor's approval.
Signed slips, vouchers and receipts, kept with the day's records.
A record of every correction, allowance and transfer, with the reason and who approved it.
The front office log, where important matters are written for the next shift.
The daily posting control sheet and night audit reports.
Records stay private. Keep them as long as the property's policy says, and then dispose of them safely.
I can explain what a folio is, and the difference between a charge and a payment.
I can explain the guest ledger and the city ledger.
I can open an account at check-in: check identity, set a credit limit, take a deposit or pre-authorisation.
I can check a charge slip for name, room, date, amount and signature before I post it.
I can post a charge, compare it with the slip, and keep the slip as proof.
I can work out a balance from charges and payments, and recognise a credit balance.
I can convert US$ to J$ and J$ to US$ at the property's rate for the day.
I can take cash and card payments correctly and give a receipt.
I can make a paid-out with the guest's signature and the receipt.
I can correct a wrong posting with a recorded adjustment, and I know which corrections need a supervisor.
I can move an account with a guest who changes rooms, and set up a split folio for a company guest.
I can use the high balance report and know what to do when a guest passes the credit limit.
I can explain what the night audit does and deal with a late charge.
I can protect account details, passwords and card information.
I can handle a disputed charge calmly and fairly.

terms: The record of a guest's charges and payments.
Adding a charge or payment to the right account.
The signed paper that proves a guest agreed to a charge.
Charges minus payments: what the guest still owes.
More has been paid than charged: the property owes the guest.
Money paid in advance; posted as a payment.
A hold on a card to cover charges; not a payment.
The most a guest may owe before being asked to pay.
Money the property pays for a guest and adds to the account.
An amount taken off an account to correct an overcharge or for poor service; needs approval.
A recorded change that corrects a wrong amount or entry.
Moving a charge from one folio to another.
An error where two digits are swapped, such as J$2,350 keyed as J$3,250.
Accounts billed later, for companies and for guests who have left owing money.
One main account for charges a company or group has agreed to pay.
Two or more folios for one guest, each with a different payer.
General Consumption Tax; charged at the current rate set by law.
The end-of-day check that balances the day's accounts.
A list of guests whose balance is near or over the credit limit.
A charge that reaches the desk after the guest has checked out.
A guest who leaves without paying.
The record of every posting and correction and who made it.
Property management system: the computer system for bookings, rooms and accounts.
Personal identification number for a card.

c1.title: Mr Whyte's stay at Treasure Beach
c1.text: Mr Andre Whyte is staying four nights at a villa in Treasure Beach at J$22,000 a night. He paid a J$30,000 deposit when he booked, and at check-in the villa placed a J$50,000 pre-authorisation on his card. After two nights his folio shows these charges: room for two nights, restaurant J$8,400, bar J$3,600, laundry J$2,200 and a boat tour J$12,000.

c2.title: A slip on the wrong room in Ocho Rios
c2.text: At a guest house in Ocho Rios, trainee Shevon posted a J$6,500 restaurant slip signed by Mrs Reid in Room 3 to the folio of Mr Campbell in Room 5. Next morning Mr Campbell asks about it at the desk. Mrs Reid has also told the desk that two minibar drinks (J$1,800) on her folio were not taken by her, because the minibar was not restocked after the last guest.

c3.title: Mrs Chen pays in US dollars
c3.text: Mrs Lisa Chen is checking out of a Negril villa. Her bill is J$63,200. She wants to pay US$300 in cash and the rest by card. The desk's made-up rate for the day is US$1 = J$158. The agent, Kemar, is new and is unsure which rate to use.

c4.title: The company guest and the credit limit
c4.text: Mr Paul Grant, a surveyor, is staying a week at a Mandeville guest house. His company, Blue Hill Surveys Ltd, has agreed in writing to pay for his room and the tax only. Mr Grant's own credit limit is J$100,000 and, after tonight's dinner, his meals and drinks bring the folio balance to J$96,500. The night auditor is preparing the reports.

c5.title: Questions at the front desk
c5.text: It is a busy afternoon at a Kingston guest house. A man phones, says he is the husband of Mrs Simone Brown in Room 6 and asks how much she has spent so far. A new colleague, Dwayne, asks to use trainee Tashoy's login 'just to save time' while his own is being set up. A guest in Room 2 asks for a printed copy of her folio for her employer.

c6.title: A bar slip after check-out
c6.text: Mr Raymond Lee checked out of a Port Antonio villa at 9:00 a.m. and paid his folio by card in full. At 11:00 a.m. the bar sends a J$2,900 slip signed by Mr Lee for drinks he had the night before. The slip was left in the bar's cash tray.

questions.q: How does Mr Whyte's J$30,000 deposit appear on his folio?
o: As a payment (credit) that lowers the balance
As a payment only once he has checked out
As a note only, because it was paid at booking
As a charge that is added to his room total
questions.why: A deposit is money the guest has already paid, so it is posted as a payment (credit). It reduces what he owes. It does not appear as a charge, and it is not left off the folio.

questions.q: After two nights, what balance does Mr Whyte owe?
questions.why: Charges: room 2 × 22,000 = 44,000, plus 8,400, 3,600, 2,200 and 12,000 = 70,200. Payments: the deposit of 30,000. Balance = 70,200 − 30,000 = J$40,200. The pre-authorisation is not a payment.

questions.q: What does the J$50,000 pre-authorisation do?
o: It pays J$50,000 towards his bill straight away
It lets the villa keep the J$50,000 if he leaves early
It holds an amount on his card to cover charges
It adds J$50,000 to his credit limit as a gift
questions.why: A pre-authorisation holds money on the card to cover what he may owe. It is not a payment: at check-out the villa charges the actual balance and the rest of the hold is released.

questions.q: Who normally posts Mr Whyte's room charge to his folio each night?
o: The housekeeper, when she has cleaned the room
The guest, by signing the registration card each day
The restaurant, when he orders his breakfast
The night audit, to every occupied room
questions.why: The night audit posts the room charge for the night to every occupied room as part of checking and balancing the day's accounts.

questions.q: Mr Campbell asks about the J$6,500 charge. What should the agent do first?
o: Ask Mr Campbell to pay it now and claim it back from the villa later
Check the signed slip, see whose it is, and tell the supervisor
Tell Mr Campbell the charge is on the system, so it must be right
Take the charge off Room 5 quietly before he sees it again
questions.why: Look at the signed slip first: it proves whose charge it is. Then correct the error openly and tell your supervisor. Never delete quietly, and never make the guest pay for a mistake the villa made.

questions.q: What is the correct way to put the J$6,500 right?
o: Post a J$6,500 allowance on Room 5 and post nothing on Room 3
Transfer it to Room 3 with a recorded reason, and keep the slip
Delete the entry from Room 5, then post a new one to Room 3 later
Leave it on Room 5 and take J$6,500 off Mrs Reid's final bill
questions.why: A wrong-room posting is corrected by moving the charge to the right folio with a recorded reason, so the audit trail shows what happened. Deleting leaves no trail, and an allowance would leave Mrs Reid's slip unpaid.

questions.q: What check would have caught Shevon's error before she posted?
o: Waiting for the night audit to look at the posting later
Asking the waiter what the guest had to eat at the meal
Comparing the room and name on the slip with the folio
Checking that the slip had the restaurant's stamp on it
questions.why: Checking the name and room on the slip against the folio, and comparing the posting with the slip afterwards, catches wrong-room errors at once. Waiting for the audit finds mistakes later, after the guest has been affected.

questions.q: Mrs Reid's J$1,800 minibar charge is to come off her account. Who must approve this?
o: Any desk agent who agrees with her about the drinks
The supervisor or manager, as an allowance
The housekeeper who checked the minibar that morning
Mr Campbell, since his folio was also affected today
questions.why: Taking a charge off an account is an allowance. It needs the approval of a supervisor or manager and a recorded reason, so that nobody can remove charges without a check.

questions.q: Which rate should Kemar use to change Mrs Chen's US$ into J$?
o: The rate he used for the last guest yesterday
The rate the property has set for today
The rate Mrs Chen says she was given at the airport
Any round rate that makes the sum easy
questions.why: The property sets a rate for each day, and everyone at the desk uses it. A different rate from a guest, from yesterday or a rate chosen for convenience would make the account wrong.

questions.q: How much J$ does Mrs Chen's US$300 cash credit to her folio?
questions.why: US$300 × 158 = J$47,400. Check the decimal point: ten times too small or too large would be badly wrong. Multiply when changing US$ into J$.

questions.q: How much J$ is left for Mrs Chen to pay by card?
Mr Grant's folio is J$3,500 below his limit and he plans to dine out again tomorrow. What is the best step for the desk?
o: Stop his key card working tonight so that he comes to the desk
Wait until the day he leaves, then ask him to settle everything
Tell the supervisor, so he can be asked privately to pay
Ask his company's staff to pay his meals without his knowledge
questions.why: A guest near the limit is reported to the supervisor, who follows the policy: a private, polite request for a payment or a higher card hold. Locking a guest out or ignoring the balance until check-out are not acceptable.

questions.q: On the second day Mr Grant has a J$3,200 breakfast at the restaurant. Which folio does the charge go to?
o: Either folio, whichever has the lower balance at the time
His personal folio, as the company pays only room and tax
The company's folio, because it pays for his visit as a whole
A new folio opened for the restaurant, to keep it apart
questions.why: A split folio sends each charge to the right payer. The company agreed to pay only the room and tax, so meals and drinks go to Mr Grant's own folio.

questions.q: What must the front office hold before the room is billed to Blue Hill Surveys Ltd?
o: Mr Grant's word that the company will pay for his room
A deposit from Mr Grant of the same amount as the room
A copy of Mr Grant's staff ID card from the company
The company's written approval of what it will pay
questions.why: A bill goes to a company only on the company's written approval, which also says exactly what it covers. Without it the property risks not being paid.

questions.q: How should the caller who says he is Mrs Brown's husband be answered?
o: Give the balance, as he knows her name and her room number
Ask him to read out her card number to prove who she is
Politely refuse and offer to take a message for her
Give only the total of the room charge for the whole stay
questions.why: Account details are private. A caller who is not the registered guest does not get them, however convincing he sounds. Offering to take a message is helpful without sharing anything.

questions.q: Why must Tashoy refuse to let Dwayne use her login?
o: The login only works on her own computer at the desk
Every posting is linked to the person who logged in
The system will charge guests twice if a login is shared
Two staff cannot use the system on the same day
questions.why: Postings and corrections are recorded under the user who logged in. If Dwayne uses her login, she is responsible for what he does and the audit trail is false.

questions.q: What should Tashoy do about the guest's request for her folio?
o: Show her the total but refuse to give her a printout
Print it once her name and key card are checked
Tell her she may have it only on the day she checks out
Email it to the employer's address she gives at the desk
questions.why: A registered guest has the right to see her own account, so print it after checking that she is that guest. Sending it to a third party would give private details to someone not authorised.

questions.q: What is the J$2,900 bar slip called, and what should the desk do with it?
o: A deposit; keep it until Mr Lee returns to the villa
A late charge; report it and follow the policy
An allowance; give it to the supervisor to throw away
A paid-out; post it to the next guest in Room 4 instead
questions.why: A charge that arrives after check-out is a late charge. Report it and follow the property's policy; do not throw it away, post it to another guest or pay it yourself.

questions.q: What would best prevent a late charge like this one in future?
o: Post all charges together at the end of the guest's stay
Charge every guest a small extra fee at check-out
Ask guests at check-out about charges made that morning
Tell the bar not to accept room charges from guests
questions.why: Asking about breakfast, minibar and other charges at check-out, and asking departments to send slips quickly, catches charges before the guest leaves. Posting late makes the problem worse.

questions.q: A bar slip for J$4,560 is keyed as J$4,650. What kind of error is this, and how is it corrected?
o: A duplicate posting; delete the whole entry and post it again
A late charge; leave it as it is and tell the guest afterwards
A wrong-room error; move the charge to another guest's folio
A transposition; post an adjustment for the J$90 difference
questions.why: Two digits have been swapped, which is a transposition. Correct it with an adjustment for the difference and record why, keeping the slip as proof. A difference that divides by 9 is a typical clue.
